name: Chester A. Arthur
summary: A New York Stalwart Republican lawyer and Custom House collector who became president after Garfield's assassination. He signed the Pendleton civil service act and began its rollout, backed rebuilding the Navy and cutting excise taxes while keeping protective duties, vetoed a 20-year Chinese immigration ban on treaty grounds but signed a 10-year one, and favored allotment and assimilation of Native Americans.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: Recommended abolishing all internal-revenue taxes except those on tobacco and liquor, and repealing stamp taxes on matches, proprietary articles and similar goods; the 1883 law cut tax and tariff receipts.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: In 1883 he said the 14th Amendment aimed to secure the colored race full civil and political rights and promised unhesitating approval of legislation guaranteeing equal enjoyment by all citizens of every right; as a lawyer he argued Lemmon v. New York for freedom of slaves brought into the state. Contested by his signing of the Chinese Exclusion Act, hence low.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Criticized dealing with tribes as separate nationalities on large reservations and urged allotment of land in severalty to dissolve the tribal bond and absorb Indians as citizens, rather than tribal authority over land.

office-by-exam.rationale: In 1881 he was cautious about competitive-only tests but pledged support if Congress adopted them; he signed the Pendleton Act (1883), named the Civil Service Commission, and in 1884 said the system fully answered its friends' expectations and that appointments came from those certified most competent by examination.

racial-franchise.rationale: In 1883 he said the 14th Amendment was meant to secure the colored race full civil and political rights, and he called for enforcement legislation; he also noted with concern that many voters could not read their ballots and urged federal aid to schools.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Vetoed the 20-year Chinese ban on treaty grounds but signed the 10-year Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) and accepted Congress's view that Chinese labor affected US interests; also enforced the 1882 Immigration Act. His record covers Chinese labor, not immigration generally.

restrict-indigenous-settlement.rationale: On 1 July 1884 he proclaimed that persons preparing an organised settlement of the Oklahoma lands in the Indian Territory would be speedily removed by the Interior Department and, if necessary, by the military, to protect the interests of the Indian nations and tribes.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: In 1884 he hoped reciprocity treaties would let 'protective duties' be retained without becoming burdensome; in 1882 he sought a substantial reduction of some duties and simplification of others, so he backed protection while seeking revision.

notes: Thin on many statement topics because his stated record is narrow. His 1881 message was cautious about competitive examinations but later he fully backed the system. Chinese exclusion and his stated support for equal civil rights point in different directions, so the equal-rights answer is low confidence. The Rivers and Harbors veto (local appropriations beyond constitutional powers) and Mongrel Tariff of 1883 matched no statement closely and were left unanswered. Later pass 2026-11-13 (rules 7): sources tagged by evidence; the five Miller Center documents not yet used (accession address, Chinese veto copy, Pan-American congress, passenger-ship veto, Nicaragua canal treaty) are read and declined with reasons, and his 1884 proclamation against settlement of the Oklahoma lands is cited as an act.
